newsitem.title: CANADA: Loewen hit by rumored profit, accounting problems.
newsitem.headline: Loewen hit by rumored profit, accounting problems.

text.p: Still reeling after fending off bankruptcy and a hostile takeover bid, Loewen Group Inc. is under attack again from a confusing barrage of rumors, denied by the company, of a looming earnings disappointment and an accounting dispute.

Shares in North America's second biggest operator of funeral homes and cemeteries have fallen more than five percent this week to their lowest level since September as investors have grown increasingly nervous.
Loewen shares dropped $1.625 to $32.625 in New York and C$2.15 to C$44.65 in Toronto on Wednesday before edging up to C44.90 in Toronto and to $32.750 in New York early on Thursday.
"There has been some modest trimming of earnings expectations and some negative sentiment surrounding the company," TD Securities analyst Darren Martin said.
Loewen narrowly escaped filing for bankruptcy last year after being slapped with $500 million of damages in a Mississippi court case.

The collapse of its stock price spurred Houston-based rival Service Corp. International to launch a $2.9 billion hostile takeover bid. Loewen defeated the bid in January and has since campaigned to rebuild investors' trust.
But the current turmoil is making shareholders edgy.

This week's pummeling of Loewen stock was triggered partly by a lowering of earnings expectations and talk that the company might not meet investors' prior profit targets. Loewen is due to report its fourth-quarter results next Wednesday.

The stock slide then gathered force largely because of murky rumors about a potential accounting problem. Various versions of the rumor have been circulating but all are untrue, said Loewen Chief Financial Officer Paul Wagler.
The talk "is totally unfounded," he said, charging that the rumors were spread by a small group of Loewen's enemies.

The rumors range from talk that Loewen and its auditors are in a dispute over the company's financial statements; that one of the company's top internal accounting officers has quit over a rift with management and that Loewen planned to change its accounting methods because it fell short of fourth-quarter earnings expectations.
"We have no disagreements or difficulty in that area," Wagler said. "Our expectation is that (earnings targets) will be achieved when results are announced."

"There was never a contemplation of changing our acounting policy. The same people have been spreading the same rumors and they are going to be terribly disappointed when we announce the results and our accountants sign off because they are in absolute and total agreement...," Wagler said.
The speculation took the heaviest toll on Loewen shares on Wednesday, the day after Service Corp. met with analysts.
Several analysts, who asked to remain anonymous, said Service highlighted what it considered to be Loewen's weaknesses and the rumors circulated at the meeting.
Nervousness over Loewen's underlying earnings performance is also worrying some investors and some analysts have lowered their forecasts in recent days.

The current consensus appears to be that Loewen will report fourth-quarter net earnings from operations of 37 to 38 cents a share or $21.5 million to $22 million. Costs associated with fighting off the Service bid are seen reducing net earnings by a further $11 million or 18 cents a share.
"The company is signaling to the street it is not going to meet the fourth-quarter numbers," said one analyst.
Wagler denied the company had changed its outlook. He said the recent lower estimates merely formalized earlier projections made by analysts.
